Volume 14 · Chapter 01

Dynamic optimization and recursive methods

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06, v09, v10, v12, v13

By the endDerive Bellman and Euler conditions and establish valid numerical solutions.

Volume 14 · Chapter 1

Prove the policy before trusting the simulation

A household decides how much to consume before next period’s income arrives. A firm decides whether to use a machine now or preserve it. Both problems require a plan for later contingencies, but neither a first-order condition nor a converged array is automatically that plan’s value. We will connect the economic feasible set, a recursive equation, a global optimality argument and an error certificate.

Capability. Build a sufficient state, prove discounted dynamic programming in a precise finite domain, derive constrained Euler conditions, verify an infinite-horizon policy using concavity and a tail condition, and distinguish iteration error from approximation error. Six original cases and twelve solved exercises prepare the stochastic-growth and incomplete-market models that follow.

Prerequisites. The resource and saving accounts of consumption and investment, conditional expectations from limit arguments and expectations, contraction and completeness, and the initial numerical Bellman treatment in numerical methods. Duality distinguishes derivative identities from global optimization; dynamic incentives supplies full contingent-plan reasoning. No general continuous-state dynamic-programming theorem is presumed here.

1. A state is a claim about information

At date t, a history ht lists observations and past actions available before the current decision. A policy selects a feasible action, possibly using a fresh random draw, from that history. It cannot use tomorrow’s shock. A proposed state st=s(ht) is sufficient for recursion only if histories with the same state have the same available actions, current reward law and conditional next-state law for each action. Time belongs in the state when remaining horizon or primitives change. A debt balance, persistent productivity, an adjustment flag or a promised continuation utility may belong there as well.

For the finite theorem below, S is a finite state set, A(s) is a nonempty finite action set, r(s,a) is a finite current utility reward, and P(s′|s,a) is a nonnegative transition row summing to one. The state is observed before a is chosen; P governs the next state after that choice. Discounting uses 0<β<1. Let B=max|r(s,a)|. The objective from initial s is Jπ(s)=Es,π∑t≥0βtr(st,at), maximized over all feasible randomized history-dependent policies. Its absolute value is at most B/(1−β). Finite histories make conditional choices and expectations elementary; we are not silently invoking a measurable selector on a general state space.

Worked case 1: the same cash, different feasible actions

A workshop has one final production decision. It owns cash 2 and observes whether its machine is cold or warm, each with probability 1/2. Operating requires a setup payment before an output receipt of 3; setup costs 3 when cold and 1 when warm. There is no borrowing. Idle retains cash. The setup provider is paid from the workshop’s cash; the later receipt cannot fund the earlier payment. In order (cash, output receipt, cold setup, warm setup), the amounts are (2,3,3,1); the warm probability is 1/2.

Cold operation is infeasible, so cold value is 2. Warm operation closes with 2−1+3=4, which beats idle. Observing and using the flag gives expected closing cash 3. A blind action required to be feasible in both states can only idle, yielding 2. These are terminal cash values, not an infinite utility stream.

A recursion on cash alone would identify two histories with different action sets. Replacing setup by its mean 2 does not repair the mistake: it authorizes an unfunded cold action. The sufficient observed state is (cash, readiness); if readiness were genuinely unobserved, the information and admissibility problem would have to be specified anew.

2. The finite discounted Bellman theorem

For a vector v∈RS, define its sup norm ||v||∞=maxs|v(s)| and the Bellman operator

(Tv)(s)=maxa∈A(s){r(s,a)+β∑s′P(s′|s,a)v(s′)}.

The continuation value is discounted once. A stationary deterministic policy σ chooses one action σ(s) in every state, including states not reached from a particular initial state. Write Tσv=rσ+βPσv. A v-greedy policy attains Tv state by state. It exists because each action set is finite. A maximizer need not be unique.

Contraction and value existence. For every action, changing v to w changes its continuation return by at most β||v−w||∞. If every member of two finite lists differs by at most d, their maxima differ by at most d: use a maximizing member of the first list for one inequality and reverse the lists for the other. Thus ||Tv−Tw||∞≤β||v−w||∞. The same proof applies to Tσ.

To prove rather than merely name the fixed-point step, start v0 arbitrary and set vn+1=Tvn. Successive distances are at most βn||Tv0−v0||∞. Summing their geometric tail makes vn Cauchy; the finite-dimensional vector space is complete. Its limit v* satisfies Tv*=v* by the displayed Lipschitz bound. Two fixed points would have distance at most β times that same distance, so coincide. Moreover ||vn−v*||∞≤βn||v0−v*||∞.

Why this is the economic value. With zero terminal payoff and n remaining decisions, backward induction gives vn=Tn0. For the inductive upper bound, condition on the first history/action; no continuation policy can beat the n−1-step value at its resulting state. Randomizing the first action only averages action returns. For attainment, choose a maximizing first action and a maximizing continuation at each successor state; the finite sets allow these choices simultaneously. Thus induction covers all contingent policies, not only stationary ones. The omitted infinite tail has absolute expectation at most Bβn/(1−β), uniformly over every admissible policy. Taking suprema preserves this bound, so the infinite-history value is the same limit v*.

Stationary recovery and verification. Pick any v*-greedy σ. Bellman’s inequality gives v*(st)≥r(st,at)+βE[v*(st+1)|ht,at] for every feasible action. Average any randomization and iterate conditional expectations. For every n, v*(s0)≥E∑t=0n−1βtrt+βnE v*(sn). The last term vanishes because v* is bounded. Equality holds throughout under σ, proving Jπ≤v*=Jσ against all histories. Conversely a stationary policy optimal in every state satisfies v*=Tσv*, so is greedy. This proves existence and recovery within the stated finite domain.

The finite formulation is also used in Sargent and Stachurski’s discrete-DP lecture, sections 11.2–11.3. The full-history and tail proof above supplies the steps needed here. For continuous states, compactness, continuity and appropriate measurability become additional questions. Lorenzoni’s Fall 2009 Lecture 9, pages 1–2 makes that broader boundary explicit. It is not proved by applying a finite grid and dropping the qualification.

3. Evaluate, improve and certify

A fixed policy solves vσ=rσ+βPσvσ. Because ||Pσ||∞=1, the matrix series ∑j≥0βjPσj converges absolutely in operator norm. Multiplying finite partial sums by I−βPσ leaves I−βn+1Pσn+1, whose last term vanishes. Hence

vσ=(I−βPσ)−1rσ,   (I−βPσ)−1=∑j≥0βjPσj≥0.

Policy iteration. Evaluate the current σ exactly, then choose a vσ-greedy σ′, keeping the old action wherever it already maximizes. Let d=Tvσ−vσ≥0. Subtract policy equations to obtain vσ′−vσ=(I−βPσ′)−1d≥0. If a policy changes under the tie rule, some d(s)>0, and the inverse’s identity term makes its value strictly improve in that state. A previously visited policy cannot return. There are finitely many deterministic stationary policies, so the procedure terminates. At termination Tvσ=vσ, which identifies v*. The proof concerns exact evaluation; floating-point linear solves require their own residual control. Without tie retention, an implementation that stops only when policy labels stop changing can cycle between equivalent labels.

Value and policy certificates. For any candidate v, its true Bellman residual is δ=||Tv−v||∞. Then ||v−v*||∞≤δ+β||v−v*||∞, so the value error is at most δ/(1−β). If a feasible policy σ is η-greedy, meaning 0≤Tv−Tσv≤η componentwise, then ||Tσv−v||∞≤δ+η. Its contraction gives ||v−vσ||∞≤(δ+η)/(1−β). Combining the two bounds yields the valid, possibly loose policy-loss certificate

0≤v*−vσ,   ||v*−vσ||∞≤(2δ+η)/(1−β).

In value iteration, ||vn+1−vn||∞ is the residual at vn, not at an arbitrarily interpolated surface. It certifies error at that vector. The next vector has error at most β times this bound. If numerical evaluation uses an approximate operator T̃, define δ̂=||T̃v−v||∞. Only a justified bound ||T̃v−Tv||∞≤εB lets us infer δ≤δ̂+εB. An action-search, interpolation or quadrature error must be included in εB; a small solver difference does not estimate it. A numerical iteration cap is an unresolved tolerance when the certificate has not passed.

The following pseudocode exposes the stopping point. actions[s] is the full finite feasible list, P[s,a,j] is the declared transition law, and norm is the sup norm. Exact arithmetic makes the printed certificates literal; a floating-point implementation must add bounds for arithmetic and linear-solve errors. The stopping tolerance is a desired value error, not a desired change between iterations.

Bellman(v):
    for s in states:
        Q[s,a] = r[s,a] + beta * sum(P[s,a,j]*v[j] for j in states)
        w[s] = max(Q[s,a] for a in actions[s])
    return w, Q

ValueIteration(v, tolerance, cap):
    for n in range(cap):
        w, Q = Bellman(v)
        delta = norm(w-v)
        if delta / (1-beta) <= tolerance:
            return v, argmax_by_state(Q), delta / (1-beta)
        v = w
    return "uncertified: iteration cap reached"

PolicyIteration(sigma):
    repeat:
        solve (I-beta*P_sigma)*v = r_sigma
        w, Q = Bellman(v)
        if w == v: return sigma, v
        for s in states:
            if Q[s,sigma[s]] < w[s]: sigma[s] = an argmax of Q[s,:]

Fixed-policy iteration can replace the linear solve: repeatedly apply Tσ, and certify its remaining error by ||Tσv−v||∞/(1−β). However, an approximately evaluated policy does not inherit exact policy iteration’s finite-termination proof automatically. One safe final check evaluates the returned feasible policy’s own residual and the full Bellman residual, accounting for both errors. The exhaustive two-state calculation next provides a reproducible small benchmark before any large grid is used.

Worked case 2: repair now or harvest repeatedly?

A device has state 0 (worn) or 1 (ready). Its reward is net service utility, not cash or a promise that finances a setup. At 0, Wait gives 1 and next state 0; Repair gives −1 and next state 1. At 1, Harvest gives 4 and next state 0; Maintain gives 2 and next state 1. These are the only feasible actions and transitions. In state order 0,1 and action order (Wait,Repair)/(Harvest,Maintain), reward rows are ((1,-1),(4,2)) and next-state indices ((0,1),(0,1)). Discount β=3/4.

Every deterministic stationary policy, evaluated exactly
Action at 0 / at 1Value (v(0),v(1))
Wait / Harvest(4,7)
Wait / Maintain(4,8)
Repair / Harvest(32/7,52/7)
Repair / Maintain(5,8)

For example, the cycling policy solves v(0)=−1+(3/4)v(1), v(1)=4+(3/4)v(0), giving the displayed fractions. Under Repair/Maintain, v(1)=2/(1−3/4)=8 and v(0)=−1+6=5. At these values, Wait gives 19/4<5 and Harvest gives 31/4<8. The policy is therefore uniquely greedy and globally optimal against every history, by the theorem. Enumerating four stationary policies would not alone have proved that last comparison without the theorem.

Policy iteration starting at Wait/Harvest evaluates (4,7). Repair then gives 17/4>4, and Maintain gives 29/4>7. Both actions change, evaluation produces (5,8), and the algorithm stops. Value iteration from zero instead gives v1=(1,4), v2=(2,5), v3=(11/4,23/4). For every n≥2,

v_n=(5,8)−3(3/4)^(n−2)(1,1).

Indeed v2 has this form, and subtracting a common constant leaves all action rankings unchanged while multiplying the constant by β. At v2, δ=3/4, so the certified and actual value error both equal 3. Its greedy policy is already optimal: a value bound need not be a sharp policy-loss estimate.

Changing β changes the economic decision as well as convergence speed. For β<2/3 the unique optimal policy is Wait/Harvest, with values (1/(1−β),(4−3β)/(1−β)). For β>2/3 it is Repair/Maintain, with values ((3β−1)/(1−β),2/(1−β)). The unused action’s gap in the first regime is 2−3β; in the second it is 3β−2. At β=2/3, values are (3,6) and every action ties; all four stationary policies are optimal. This is not a claim that an optimal physical state path or invariant distribution must be unique.

4. Euler equations are local resource comparisons

Now use a continuous scalar capital choice. Let zt be an observed exogenous shock with finitely many successors at each finite history. Its transition probabilities do not change when capital changes. At date t, capital kt was chosen earlier, zt is observed, and the household selects kt+1 and consumes ct subject to

c_t+k_(t+1)=f(k_t,z_t),   c_t>0,   k_(t+1)≥0.

The function f includes output plus any surviving capital; it must not be counted a second time. Utility is ∑βtu(ct), with u increasing and differentiable at the positive consumptions considered. Capital and consumption are adapted: kt+1 can use date-t information, not zt+1. We may additionally impose a fixed cap kt+1≤K. For this local necessity derivation, the candidate has a finite objective and f is differentiable at its next capital; a path whose objective is −∞ cannot be declared locally optimal from an unchanged infinite tail.

At a positive-probability history, increase kt+1 by a small d, reducing ct by d. Keep kt+2 and all later contingent capital choices fixed on each successor shock branch; next consumption changes to first order by fk(kt+1,zt+1)d. With positive consumption on the finitely many immediate successors, sufficiently small permitted d preserves feasibility. Differentiating this finite perturbation requires no derivative of a value function or infinite-sum interchange. Its conditional marginal payoff, divided by βt, is

−u′(c_t)+β E_t[u′(c_(t+1)) f_k(k_(t+1),z_(t+1))].

At an interior choice both signs of d are available, so this quantity is zero. At kt+1=0 only an increase is available and it must be nonpositive: u′(ct)≥βEt[u′(ct+1)fk]. At a binding positive fixed upper cap only a decrease is available, so the inequality reverses. These signs assume no other binding constraint; additional restrictions require their own feasible directions. The return belongs inside the expectation when it is random or correlated with marginal utility. For financial saving ct+at+1=R at+yt, at+1≥0, the same argument replaces fk by R.

Terminal conditions. With a last consumption date T, no terminal benefit and no obligation to preserve capital, strict monotonicity makes kT+1=0: consuming any unused terminal resource improves utility. If the objective instead includes βT+1S(kT+1), the interior terminal condition is u′(cT)=βS′(kT+1), with the corresponding endpoint inequalities. A finite model’s terminal condition is part of its economic specification. Setting capital to zero at a distant numerical endpoint is an approximation to an infinite model, not its transversality theorem.

Lorenzoni’s Fall 2009 Lecture 5, pages 1–3 treats the growth budget and interior marginal conditions. We derive the discount factor directly: the stochastic Euler equality is u′(ct)=βEt[u′(ct+1)fk], not that expression with β dropped.

5. Concavity plus a tail condition gives sufficiency

Here is a sufficient-condition theorem with its domain exposed. Shocks have finite support at every finite history and follow the same exogenous law under every policy. Fix initial capital and shock information. For each z, f(·,z) is concave on a nonnegative capital domain and has a finite supporting derivative at each candidate k*t; u is increasing, concave and differentiable at c*t>0. All finite-horizon quantities used below are integrable. The objective is defined as the limit of expected discounted partial utility sums: assume this limit exists for each admissible adapted feasible policy, taking values in R∪{−∞}, and is finite for the candidate. This explicitly excludes undefined ∞−∞ objectives. When positive utility parts have a summable expected bound, that limit agrees with the expected infinite series by monotone convergence applied to the negative parts.

Assume the candidate satisfies the preceding conditional Euler equality at interior capital and the stated inequalities at a zero lower bound or a fixed upper cap. Finally require

lim_(T→∞) E[β^T u′(c*_T) k*_(T+1)]=0.

Then the candidate is globally optimal within that admissible class. This is a proved sufficient transversality condition, not a claim that exactly this condition is necessary in every infinite-horizon model. Nonnegative comparison capital and the existence of the objective limit matter.

Proof. Compare any other feasible adapted (k,c), and put Δkt=kt−k*t. Concavity and positive marginal utility give, at each history,

u(c_t)−u(c*_t)≤u′(c*_t)(c_t−c*_t)≤u′(c*_t)[f_k(k*_t,z_t)Δk_t−Δk_(t+1)].

Multiply by βt, sum t=0,…,T, and take expectations. The initial difference is zero. For every internal t≥1, Δkt is known at date t−1; the tower property changes its coefficient to

β^(t−1){β E_(t−1)[u′(c*_t)f_k(k*_t,z_t)]−u′(c*_(t−1))}Δk_t.

This is zero for an interior candidate. At its zero lower bound the bracket is nonpositive and Δkt≥0; at its upper cap the bracket is nonnegative and Δkt≤0. Every internal term is therefore nonpositive. The remaining endpoint gives

E∑_(t=0)^T β^t[u(c_t)−u(c*_t)]≤−E[β^T u′(c*_T)Δk_(T+1)]≤E[β^T u′(c*_T)k*_(T+1)].

The second inequality uses comparison capital kT+1≥0. Taking limits establishes that its value cannot exceed the candidate’s. A competitor of value −∞ is already dominated. No expectation/limit interchange beyond the explicitly defined objective is concealed in this final step. For a deterministic model remove all expectations; the proof is identical.

The concavity/tail method appears in Lorenzoni’s Fall 2009 Lecture 6, section 1. The proof here includes conditional expectations, binding-boundary signs and objective convergence explicitly. It is distinct from the bounded-value remainder in Section 2: an unbounded marginal utility or state cannot be discarded by saying β<1.

Worked case 3: log growth, with the missing verification supplied

Consider f(k)=A kα, u(c)=log c, A>0, 0<α<1, 0<β<1, initial k0>0. Feasible infinite plans have ct>0, kt+1>0 and ct+kt+1=A ktα. Setting next capital to zero would make all subsequent positive consumption impossible. Actions (0,f(k)) form an open interval and rewards tend to −∞ near zero consumption. The finite bounded-reward contraction theorem does not apply.

Let s=αβ, b=α/(1−s), and a=[log((1−s)A)+βb log(sA)]/(1−β). The proposed policy and value are g(k)=sA kα, c(k)=(1−s)A kα, V(k)=a+b log k. Substituting the candidate continuation into log(f(k)−x)+βV(x) gives a strictly concave function of x∈(0,f(k)), tending to −∞ at both endpoints. Its first-order equation 1/(f(k)−x)=βb/x has the unique global solution x=s f(k). Matching the constant and log-k coefficients gives the displayed a,b. A formal Bellman solution has now been found; it still needs an infinite-horizon verification.

For any feasible plan, kt≤K=max{k0,A1/(1−α)} by induction, and ct≤K. Thus log-positive parts are bounded above by max{log K,0}, making every objective well-defined as a finite number or −∞. Along the candidate, log kt+1=log(sA)+α log kt; its explicit geometric solution is bounded, so its log consumption and objective are finite. It satisfies the Euler equality, since βf′(k′)/c(k′)=αβ/[(1−s)k′]=1/c(k). Its shadow-value tail is βTkT+1/cT=βTs/(1−s)→0. The sufficiency theorem now proves optimality against every feasible plan, not just among log-affine guesses. Iterating the candidate Bellman identity has a vanishing βnV(kn) because its log states are bounded, confirming that V equals its attained objective.

For (A,α,β,k0)=(2,1/2,3/4,16), saving share is 3/8, coefficient b=4/5, and a=4 log(5/4)+(12/5)log(3/4). The first resource split is (k1,c0)=(3,5); the next is k2=3√3/4, c1=5√3/4. Here 1/c0=1/5 equals (3/4)(1/√3)/(5√3/4). The steady pair is (k,c)=(9/16,15/16), and V(16)≈2.4202082091643895. The tail is (3/5)(3/4)T. Convergence of this specific capital path follows from the log recurrence with coefficient α; it is not a consequence of Bellman contraction alone.

6. Boundaries that change the answer

Worked case 4: saving at a borrowing limit

A household has two consumption dates, log utility and β=1/2. It owns m at date 0, saves a with 0≤a<m at gross return R=1, and receives terminal labor income y∈(1,4) with probabilities (1/2,1/2). These are stipulated funded wage receipts, observed only at date 1; there is no borrowing or remaining terminal asset. Its budgets are c0=m−a and c1=a+y. Compare initial endowments m=(2,4); the higher endowment is a different environment, not a costless policy recommendation.

The objective is F(a)=log(m−a)+(1/4)log(a+1)+(1/4)log(a+4). Its second derivative is strictly negative throughout [0,m), and F→−∞ as a→m. Thus a derivative sign at zero or the unique interior root establishes the global optimum. At m=2, F′(0)=−1/2+5/16=−3/16<0, so a*=0. The Euler comparison is (1/2,5/16), with a strict inequality. Forcing equality would demand an unavailable negative saving choice.

In general F′(0)=−1/m+5/16. The corner persists exactly for m≤16/5, including equality because the derivative subsequently decreases. At m=4, multiplying the interior equation by its positive denominators gives 6a²+17a−4=0. The negative root is infeasible; the optimum is (sqrt(385)−17)/12≈0.21845140586238188, strictly between 0 and 4.

Replacing uncertain y by its mean 5/2 would instead give derivative −1/4+(1/2)/(5/2)=−1/20 at zero, hence a*=0 at m=4. The original risky household saves strictly more here. The underlying inequality is E[1/(a+y)]>1/(a+E y), because reciprocal consumption is strictly convex and the income law is nondegenerate. This two-date example is not a general precautionary-saving theorem for every preference, return or borrowing constraint.

Worked case 5: a feasible Euler path that is not optimal

Let ct+kt+1=2kt, k0=2, kt+1≥0 and ct>0, with u=log and (β,R,k0)=(1/2,2,2). Euler equality requires ct+1=βR ct=ct. The constant path ct=1 is feasible with kt=1+2t; its value is 0. But ct=2, kt=2 is also feasible and gives value 2log(2)>0.

The bad path’s shadow tail is 2−T(1+2T+1)→2; the good path’s is 2−T→0. The initial capital is not exhausted in present-value consumption under the bad path: ∑ct/2t+1=1<2. These are real goods carried forward, not an unpaid external debt. Nonnegative capital ensures feasibility but does not force optimal use of owned resources.

The sufficiency theorem verifies the good path. For every feasible competitor kt≤2t+1, so log-positive consumption is bounded by a constant times t+1 and its discounted sum is finite. The objective therefore exists in R∪{−∞}; linear f is concave, Euler holds, and the good tail vanishes. This supplies global optimality without applying a bounded-reward sup-norm argument to an unbounded domain.

Worked case 6: a zero residual for the wrong operator

In the device problem, suppose a routine evaluates T̃v=Tv+εB(1,1), with the known offset εB=1/20. Because T(v+c1)=Tv+βc1, its fixed point is v*+εB/(1−β)·1=(26/5,41/5). The computed residual is zero, but the true residual is 1/20 and true value error 1/5. The operator-error bound restores the correct certificate. The policy remains optimal in this special common-offset case because all actions’ continuation values shift equally; that fact does not license ignoring other approximation errors.

A second model has one state, β=3/4 and two actions with rewards (0,1), each returning to that state. A coarse action list containing only reward 0 converges to value 0 and reports residual 0 on its own problem. The true value is 4, and its true residual at zero is 1. The selected coarse policy loses 4. The missing action is a modeling/optimization error; more iterations of that action list cannot repair it.

Finally, contraction need not imply attainment outside the finite action domain. With one state, actions a∈[0,1), reward a and β=3/4, T v=supa(a+βv)=1+βv has the unique fixed point 4. Every policy’s first expected reward is strictly below 1, so no policy attains 4, even if later actions approach one. Constant a=1−ε policies approach the supremum. A max sign would hide the missing maximizer. This boundary is solved in Exercise 11.

7. Transfer exercises and complete solutions

Give the admissible information and feasible set before optimizing. A theorem name, a numerical output or an Euler equality without its relevant conditions is not a full answer. Exercise 12 is a research critique with an explicit rubric; the remaining questions have determinate mathematical answers.

  1. In the workshop case, identify a sufficient observed state and its feasible action sets. Compute the conditional and ex-ante optimal values and the best single action feasible in both histories. A manager replaces setup by its mean and reports an expected closing balance of three. Is that calculation a feasible policy? Explain how a genuinely unobserved readiness flag changes the problem specification.
  2. Prove that Tn0 equals the n-date value over all randomized history-dependent policies in the finite model. Derive a uniform bound between that value and the infinite value from B=max|r|. Show why a stationary maximizer of the fixed-point equation attains the infinite value. Identify the exact step at which boundedness is used, and why log growth cannot simply be substituted.
  3. Reconstruct all four policy values and one policy-iteration step in the device model from its resource-free service rewards. Now repair succeeds with probability 3/4 and otherwise leaves the device worn; its reward remains −1. Every other primitive is unchanged. Find the new optimal policy/value. For general success probability p∈[0,1], derive the threshold and all stationary optimal policies at equality.
  4. Return to certain repair, and let 0<β<1 vary. Derive the full set of optimal deterministic stationary policies below, above and at the switching discount factor. Prove the inequalities for both states; comparing only the initial-state value is insufficient. At the switch, can a randomized history-dependent policy be suboptimal?
  5. For value iteration from zero at β=3/4, prove the full formula for every n≥2, the exact error and the residual at vn. Find the first n for which the certified value error is at most 1/10. Explain precisely which iterate the code in Section 3 returns and why the policy may be correct long before its value is accurate. Derive a residual certificate for iterative fixed-policy evaluation.
  6. Prove the certificate using computed residual δ̂ and operator bound εB, and the η-greedy policy-loss bound. Reconstruct both false-zero-residual examples from their primitives. Explain whether the common operator offset must change the optimal policy, and why an omitted feasible action requires more than a smaller iteration tolerance.
  7. For the general log/Cobb growth problem, derive both value coefficients and the saving rule from the Bellman guess. Prove the global stage optimum and infinite-horizon verification separately. Reconstruct the numeric first two capital/consumption splits, steady pair and value at k0=16. State a bound ensuring competitors have defined objectives and prove the candidate tail condition.
  8. Derive conditional Euler equality and both bound inequalities using a finite two-date adapted perturbation, without differentiating a value function. Explain the sign of each internal term in the concavity sufficiency proof. As a finite-horizon transfer, a terminal household has resources 5, β=1/2, u(c)=log c, and salvage S(x)=log(1+x), paid as discounted terminal utility. Solve max0≤x<5{log(5−x)+(1/2)log(1+x)}. Derive the complete solution for resources M>0 and identify the endpoint threshold.
  9. Solve the risky two-date saving problem for every m>0: give the corner threshold and positive-root formula above it. Verify the specified m=2 and m=4 decisions. Derive the solution under certain income equal to the risky mean, and compare the two thresholds. Explain exactly which convexity property accounts for the discrepancy here.
  10. In the linear log problem, characterize every strictly positive constant-consumption path satisfying feasibility and Euler equality. Derive its capital path, present-value consumption, attained utility and shadow-tail limit. Use a finite telescoping budget and the supporting inequality for log to prove the globally optimal path and its uniqueness among all feasible paths, not only constant ones.
  11. For the one-state model with a∈[0,1), reward a and β=3/4, prove contraction and identify the infinite value supremum. Prove that no randomized history-dependent policy attains it. For any prescribed value gap ε>0, construct a stationary policy with gap at most ε. Explain which finite-theorem hypothesis has been dropped and why contraction remains true.
  12. Referee this fictional report: “Our grid iteration changed by less than 10−8, so the continuous-model policy is within 10−8 of optimal. Its Euler residual is zero, proving optimality even at a borrowing constraint. The cash balance automatically contains all relevant information. A stationary optimal policy implies that every economy converges to one deterministic steady state.” Supply a precise counterexample to each inference from this chapter and specify a minimal valid replacement claim with the evidence it needs. Grade the report’s mathematical logic, not its policy conclusion.
Complete solutions and critique rubric

  1. The state is (cash, readiness) at this final date. At (2,cold), only Idle is feasible since setup three exceeds two; at (2,warm), Idle and Operate are feasible since setup one is affordable. Closing balances from the optimal choices are two and four, respectively. Their equal-probability expectation is three. An action feasible in both states must be Idle, giving two. Average setup two produces the arithmetic 2−2+3=3, but does not pay the actual cold bill of three when only two is available. Equality of an expected number with the observed-policy value is not implementation.

    If readiness is unobserved, a belief over readiness may become a state, but that alone does not say whether attempting operation can fail, whether setup is learned before payment, or whether statewise insolvency is allowed. Under the prompt’s requirement that the chosen action be feasible in both histories, only Idle is available. A contract that funds cold operation or a learning action changes the feasible set and needs new resources/information; it cannot be inferred from taking an average.

  2. At zero remaining dates the payoff is zero. Suppose vn−1 is the attainable best continuation from every state. For any first action at s, conditional expected payoff is at most r(s,a)+β∑P(s′|s,a)vn−1(s′). Randomizing makes a convex combination, no larger than the maximum. A maximizing first action exists; selecting an attaining n−1-date continuation separately at each of finitely many successor states achieves that maximum. This inductively constructs a policy contingent on current state and remaining time and bounds every history-dependent policy. Hence vn=Tvn−1.

    For any infinite policy, the omitted tail has absolute value at most ∑t=n∞βtB=Bβn/(1−β). Conversely, every finite policy has an infinite extension because all action sets are nonempty. Taking suprema therefore gives ||vn−J*||∞≤Bβn/(1−β). Contraction makes vn converge to v*. For a stationary greedy σ, iterate v*=Tσv*: v*(s)=E∑t<nβtrt+βnE v*(sn). The remainder vanishes because the finite vector v* is bounded, proving attainment. The same expression is an inequality for other policies. Bounded rewards enter the uniform objective-tail bound, and bounded v* enters verification. Log rewards on open consumption sets have no finite B; merely discounting does not supply either bound there.

  3. Write w,h for the values at worn and ready. Wait/Harvest gives w=1+(3/4)w=4 and h=4+(3/4)w=7. Wait/Maintain retains w=4 and gives h=2+(3/4)h=8. Repair/Harvest gives w=−1+(3/4)h and h=4+(3/4)w, hence (w,h)=(32/7,52/7). Repair/Maintain gives (5,8). From (4,7), Repair’s return is 17/4>4 and Maintain’s is 29/4>7; simultaneous improvement gives Repair/Maintain. At (5,8), alternatives give 19/4 and 31/4, both strictly lower, so the policy is fixed.

    With success p and Maintain, h=8 and w=−1+(3/4)[(1−p)w+8p], hence w=(24p−4)/(1+3p). Repair is better than Wait at this value exactly when w>4, equivalent to p>2/3. Maintain beats Harvest throughout p∈[2/3,1], since w≤5 and 8−(4+3w/4)≥1/4. For p<2/3, Wait/Maintain gives (4,8); the alternative repair return is 2+3p<4 and Harvest gives seven<eight. At p=2/3 either action at worn is optimal, while Maintain is uniquely optimal at ready; exactly two deterministic stationary policies are optimal. At p=3/4 the value is (56/13,8), with strict Repair/Maintain. The two unused-action gaps there are (1/13,10/13). Keeping Harvest optimal from the deterministic model after changing success would be an invalid transfer.

  4. Evaluate Wait/Harvest at general β: w=1/(1−β), h=(4−3β)/(1−β). The gap between its chosen action and the alternative is w−(−1+βh)=2−3β at worn and h−(2+βh)=2−3β at ready. Thus it is uniquely greedy when β<2/3. Repair/Maintain gives h=2/(1−β), w=(3β−1)/(1−β). Its gaps are w−(1+βw)=3β−2 and h−(4+βw)=3β−2. Thus it is uniquely greedy when β>2/3. In each regime the Bellman theorem proves global optimality; conversely every optimal stationary policy must be greedy at the unique value, so no other such policy qualifies.

    At β=2/3 both expressions give (3,6), and each of the four action returns equals its state value. All four deterministic stationary policies, every stationary mixture, and indeed every feasible randomized history-dependent policy are optimal. To prove the last assertion, Bellman verification has equality at every selected action and a uniformly vanishing remainder. A tie in one calculation does not automatically justify all histories; that verification is the missing step.

  5. Direct application of the operator gives v1=(1,4), v2=(2,5) and v3=(11/4,23/4). For a scalar d, stochastic rows imply T(v*−d1)=v*−βd1. Starting with v2=v*−3·1, induction gives vn=v*−3(3/4)n−21 for every n≥2. Consequently the exact error is 3(3/4)n−2 and the residual is (3/4)(3/4)n−2; dividing by 1−β gives equality in the value certificate.

    The first qualifying index is 14. Indeed the error at n=13 is 531441/4194304>1/10, while the error at n=14 is 1594323/16777216<1/10; errors decrease strictly. The loop starts with v=v0. At loop index fourteen, it forms v15 to measure the residual at v14 and returns v14, its greedy policy and its certificate, provided the cap permits that index. The first loop label and the count of Bellman calls are different: fifteen calls are needed. Every vn for n≥2 is v* minus a common constant, so its greedy policy is already optimal. At v1 Harvest is greedy at ready; it is not yet the optimal full policy.

    For a fixed σ, contraction gives ||v−vσ||∞≤||v−Tσv||∞+β||v−vσ||∞, hence its own residual divided by 1−β bounds evaluation error. An accurate fixed-policy value alone does not establish that policy’s optimality: the full action set must still be compared.

  6. The triangle inequality yields ||Tv−v||∞≤||Tv−T̃v||∞+||T̃v−v||∞≤εB+δ̂. Contraction then gives ||v−v*||∞≤(δ̂+εB)/(1−β). For an η-greedy feasible σ, ||Tσv−v||∞≤δ+η, so ||v−vσ||∞≤(δ+η)/(1−β). Combining with the value bound proves ||v*−vσ||∞≤(2δ+η)/(1−β), or ≤[2(δ̂+εB)+η]/(1−β). The componentwise lower bound v*≥vσ follows from the all-policy value theorem. An approximate greedy choice needs a bound relative to the true action returns; a computed argmax alone does not make η zero.

    For the offset εB=1/20, solve c=βc+εB: c=1/5, so the perturbed value is (26/5,41/5). The computed residual is zero and the true residual is ||−(1−β)c1||∞=1/20; the true error is 1/5. All actions gain the same βc in their continuation return, so their rankings and the optimal policy are unchanged here. For the one-state omitted-action problem, the true equation is v=1+3v/4, yielding four, whereas the coarse equation v=3v/4 yields zero. At zero the true residual is one and the coarse residual zero. Choosing reward zero loses four forever. An operator-error analysis must include the omitted gain; running the coarse iteration longer cannot make that gain disappear.

  7. Substitute V(k)=a+b log k into the stage objective log(Akα−x)+βa+βb log x. Matching the log-k coefficient after optimizing requires b=α(1+βb), hence b=α/(1−αβ)>0. The objective has second derivative −1/(Akα−x)²−βb/x²<0 and tends to −∞ at either endpoint. Its unique optimizer solves x=βb(Akα−x), giving x=αβAkα. Set s=αβ. The constant equation is (1−β)a=log((1−s)A)+βb log(sA). This proves a globally maximizing stage choice for the proposed continuation function, not yet the infinite optimum.

    For any feasible plan, choose K=max{k0,A1/(1−α)}; k≤K implies Akα≤K, so all states and consumptions are at most K. Positive log utility is therefore bounded by max{log K,0}, and its discounted sum is finite. Negative parts may diverge, yielding an admissible value −∞, but never an undefined difference of infinities. Along the candidate, log kt=αtlog k0+(1−αt)log(sA)/(1−α), a bounded sequence. Candidate consumption logs and value are finite. Direct substitution gives 1/ct=βf′(kt+1)/ct+1, and its tail is βTs/(1−s)→0. The concavity/tail proof applies to every feasible competitor. Iterating the attained Bellman identity and using bounded candidate log capital identifies its objective with a+b log k0.

    At the specified primitives s=3/8, b=4/5, a=4log(5/4)+(12/5)log(3/4), k1=3,c0=5 and (k2,c1)=(3√3/4,5√3/4). The fixed capital solves √k=3/4, giving k=9/16 and c=15/16. V(16)≈2.4202082091643895. The boundedness along this candidate is proved from its log recurrence; it was not inferred from bounded rewards, which fail on the whole action domain.

  8. At a positive-probability date-t history, alter the single measurable decision kt+1 by d, leave each successor’s kt+2 fixed, and leave later decisions fixed. Consumption today falls by d; successor consumption changes by fkd to first order. There are finitely many immediate successors and positive candidate consumptions, so sufficiently small permitted d is feasible on all of them. Dividing the conditional payoff derivative by βt yields D=−u′(ct)+βEt[u′(ct+1)fk]. Both signs permitted implies D=0. At a zero lower bound, only d≥0 is permitted, implying D≤0. At an upper cap, only d≤0 is permitted, implying D≥0. These are necessary local comparisons for a finite-valued optimum, not a global verification without concavity/tail restrictions.

    In the sufficiency sum the internal coefficient is βt−1Dt−1Δkt. At a lower bound Δk≥0 and D≤0, so their product is nonpositive; at the cap Δk≤0 and D≥0, again nonpositive. Interior products vanish. Only −βTu′(c*T)ΔkT+1 remains; nonnegative comparison capital bounds it by the candidate’s shadow tail. This explains why lower-bound signs must not be reversed.

    The terminal objective has derivative −1/(M−x)+(1/2)/(1+x) and strictly negative second derivative. At zero its derivative is −1/M+1/2, so the unique optimizer is zero for M≤2. For M>2 the interior equation 2(1+x)=M−x gives x=(M−2)/3, which lies in (0,M). The objective tends to −∞ at x→M, so this maximizer is global. At M=5, (x,c)=(1,4), and both marginal sides equal 1/4. With no salvage, every positive x wastes terminal resources and x=0. Salvage is part of the objective, not an infinite-horizon TVC.

  9. The derivative is −1/(m−a)+(1/4)/(a+1)+(1/4)/(a+4), strictly decreasing because F″<0. At zero it is −1/m+5/16, nonpositive iff m≤16/5. At equality the derivative immediately becomes negative, so zero is still the unique maximizer. Above the threshold, continuity and F′→−∞ at a→m give one root. Clearing the positive denominators yields 6a²+(25−2m)a+16−5m=0. Its constant term is negative when m>16/5, so its two roots have opposite signs. The positive root is

    a*(m)=[2m−25+sqrt(4m²+20m+241)]/12.

    The derivative argument proves this root is strictly below m. At m=2 the optimum is zero; at m=4 the polynomial is 6a²+17a−4 and the root is (√385−17)/12≈0.21845140586238188.

    With income certain at 5/2, the derivative is −1/(m−a)+(1/2)/(a+5/2). Its corner threshold is 5, and above it the interior equation 2a+5=m−a gives a=(m−5)/3. Thus at m=4 the mean-income economy saves zero while the risky economy saves positively. For any feasible a, strict convexity of x↦1/x gives E[1/(a+y)]>1/(a+E y), increasing the marginal gain to saving under the specified income risk. This compares two utility expectations within a two-date log model; it does not establish an unrestricted theorem under different preferences or endogenous returns.

  10. Euler equality gives ct+1=βRct=ct. Write this positive constant as C. Solving kt+1=2kt−C from k0=2 gives kt=C+(2−C)2t. It remains nonnegative at every date iff 0<C≤2; if C>2 the negative exponential coefficient eventually makes capital negative. Present-value consumption is ∑C/2t+1=C; utility is 2log C. Its shadow tail is 2−T[C+(2−C)2T+1]/C, with limit 2(2−C)/C. Only C=2 has a zero tail; C=1 has limit two and value zero.

    For any feasible path, divide the budget by 2t+1 and telescope: ∑t=0Tct/2t+1+kT+1/2T+1=2. Thus the infinite present-value consumption sum is at most two. The supporting inequality log c≤log2+(c−2)/2 implies, after multiplying by 2−t and summing finite terms, a utility difference bounded in the limit by ∑ct/2t+1−2≤0. The objective limit is legitimate because ct≤2t+2 bounds discounted positive log parts by a summable multiple of t+2; a value −∞ is dominated automatically. The path c=2,k=2 attains 2log2, hence is globally optimal.

    For uniqueness, define d(c)=log2+(c−2)/2−log c≥0, strictly positive unless c=2. The same inequality, retaining one date’s strictly positive discounted gap, shows that any path differing from two at any date has strictly lower utility (or −∞). Thus the optimal consumption path is unique, and its budget fixes the capital path. The budget proof distinguishes leaving wealth unused from violating feasibility.

  11. For any finite scalar v, sup0≤a<1(a+3v/4)=1+3v/4. Thus |Tv−Tw|=(3/4)|v−w| and its unique fixed point is four. Every policy has payoff at most ∑(3/4)t=4. To see strictness even under randomization, the first action A0<1 almost surely has E(1−A0)>0. Indeed the union over positive integers n of {1−A0≥1/n} has probability one, so at least one such event has positive probability. Expected loss at date zero is strictly positive and all later losses are nonnegative, implying J<4.

    Given ε>0, set d=min{1/2,ε/4} and choose constant action a=1−d. It is feasible, with value (1−d)/(1−3/4)=4−4d and gap 4d≤ε. Hence the value supremum is exactly four but unattained. Finite action sets, which ensured an attaining maximizer, have been replaced by a nonclosed infinite set. Boundedness and discounting still make this operator a contraction; neither property supplies a missing maximizing action.

  12. Benchmark critique. First, an iterate change can be an operator residual only at a specified vector and for a specified operator. Even the true residual needs division by 1−β for value error, and policy loss needs its own bound. Case 6 has zero computed residual but true value error 1/5 under the known offset; omitted actions give error four. A valid continuous-model claim requires a justified approximation/operator bound on the relevant domain, a solver residual, and a true-action greediness bound. With unbounded rewards it also needs an appropriate domain-specific verification theorem, not the finite theorem’s name.

    Second, case 5 has a feasible exact Euler path with utility zero below 2log2. Conversely, case 4 at m=2 has an optimal strict Euler inequality, so forcing equality can reject an optimum. A valid replacement states feasible directions, correct boundary complementarity, and either a valid dynamic-programming verification or the chapter’s concavity, objective-convergence and tail hypotheses.

    Third, case 1 has identical cash but different feasible actions; the cold setup is unfunded if the flag is dropped. A sufficient state must preserve feasible sets, rewards and conditional transitions under each action, with time/beliefs/promises included when the model requires them. Testing a trajectory does not prove that property.

    Fourth, at β=2/3 in the deterministic device model, Repair/Harvest is stationary and optimal, yet its physical state alternates forever between zero and one. It does not converge to one deterministic steady state. An optimal policy also may admit multiple recurrent classes or persistent exogenous shocks. The Bellman theorem proves value and policy properties; a long-run distribution or path claim needs a separate transition analysis and its assumptions.

    Ten-point rubric. Award two points for each of the four numbered inference repairs: one for a concrete valid witness and one for the required replacement hypotheses/evidence. Award one additional point for explicitly separating value error, policy loss and physical-path convergence, and one for preserving the stated economic model when proposing a numerical repair. A new borrowing opportunity, hidden transfer or deterministic shock is a changed model and earns no repair point unless labeled as such. A response can recommend further research or rejection; that judgment receives no automatic points. The exact contradictions and proof boundaries determine the score.

8. Explain, retain and carry the tools forward

Teach-back. In two minutes explain (i) why a state is more than a convenient variable list, (ii) how a Bellman fixed point becomes an attained value, (iii) why an Euler equation can reject a correct corner or admit a wrong path, and (iv) what a numerical residual certifies. Use one concrete case for each.

Teach-back benchmark

A state must preserve the decision problem conditional on information: cash alone fails for the workshop because it drops readiness-dependent financing feasibility. For finite states/actions, contraction gives a unique bounded fixed point; a maximizing policy exists, and iterating Bellman inequalities with a vanishing discounted remainder verifies it against all histories. Those are separate steps. The risky saver at m=2 optimally chooses zero with a strict Euler inequality, while the linear-growth saver consuming one satisfies equality but leaves a positive shadow tail and is suboptimal. A true residual δ certifies value error δ/(1−β) in the stated contraction domain; approximate operators require an additional error bound, and policy loss requires a feasible policy and its greediness error. Zero residual for an omitted-action problem certifies only that smaller problem.

Delayed retention. After two days, without consulting the chapter: derive the inequality sign at an upper saving cap; recover the device value at β=3/4 from its two equations; state the hypotheses that let the log-growth verification work; and diagnose a zero residual from an action grid that omits a profitable choice. After two weeks, rederive the full-history Bellman verification and the finite partial-sum sufficiency inequality, then solve the terminal salvage problem at general M.

Retention answers

At an upper cap, only decreasing saving is feasible, so D=−u′+βE[u′f′]≥0 and u′≤βE[u′f′]. Device Maintain gives h=2+(3/4)h=8; Repair gives w=−1+(3/4)8=5; the other actions are strictly worse. Log-growth verification uses positive feasible consumption/capital, concavity, a finite-valued candidate, defined competitor objectives ensured by bounded positive utility parts, the correct Euler condition and βTkT+1/cT→0. Missing a reward-one action from the one-state reward-zero grid produces computed value zero, true value four and true residual one.

For the later session, Bellman inequalities telescope to a finite reward sum plus βnE v*(sn), whose bounded-value remainder vanishes. Concavity and conditional Euler signs instead bound each finite utility difference by E[βTu′(c*T)k*T+1]; a stated shadow-tail condition makes that bound vanish. The two proofs control different remainders. Terminal salvage yields x*=0 for M≤2 and (M−2)/3 for M>2, with consumption M−x*, by strict concavity and the derivative sign.

Bridge. The next chapter adds observed productivity and labor to stochastic growth. It must specify a sufficient state, preserve the shock timing, and include labor’s marginal condition alongside the capital Euler condition; the present finite theorem does not itself prove the continuous model. The incomplete-market chapter then adds individual asset constraints and a distribution of households. Its numerical work must distinguish household value/policy error, distributional approximation and market-clearing error. An invariant distribution, a competitive equilibrium and a policy fixed point are different mathematical objects, each needing its own existence or verification argument.

Sources and further study

  • Sargent and Stachurski — QuantEcon, Discrete State Dynamic Programming — Author-led extension to stochastic finite-state Bellman problems; this library uses its own deterministic example and standard-library code.
  • Guido Lorenzoni — MIT 14.451 Lecture Notes 5: Optimal Growth Model (Fall 2009) — Owned production/consumption budget and the distinction between positive consumption, envelope conditions and Euler equations.
  • Guido Lorenzoni — MIT 14.451 Lecture Notes 6: Euler Equations (Fall 2009) — Concavity and a vanishing nonnegative-capital shadow-value tail as a sufficiency route. Our finite-shock conditional proof states all expectation and tail hypotheses.
  • Guido Lorenzoni — MIT 14.451 Lecture Notes 9: Stochastic Dynamic Programming (Fall 2009) — State includes observed Markov shock; finite shock histories versus general measurable-state models.
